If the participant did not score a three in the first in situ assessment, a booster session of small-scale simulation training was provided. If the participant did not score 3 after two booster sessions, the researcher conducted IST. If IST was not effective, a reinforcement procedure was implemented.

documents.title: Evaluating small-scale simulation training of firearm safety to children with autism spectrum disorder: Method › Procedure › Baseline
documents.content: Baseline data consisted of both in situ assessments and simulation assessments. No feedback or consequences were delivered to the participant by either the researcher or caregiver. Caregivers were trained using BST to ensure that they were prepared for what to do based on the participant's performance during an assessment. If the child left the room and told the parent about the gun, the parent thanked the child for telling and then went into the room, picked the gun up, and put it away in another room. If the child did not leave the room in 30 s after orienting in the direction of the gun, the parent entered the room. Regardless of whether the child was not touching the gun, touching the gun, or playing with the gun, the parent calmly walked up to the gun, picked it up (or took it from the child's hands), and said in a neutral tone of voice, "I better put this gun away," while walking from the room with the gun. The parent did not discuss the gun further with the child. The parent engaged in this behavior during in situ assessments in baseline and the small-scale simulation training intervention.

documents.title: Evaluating small-scale simulation training of firearm safety to children with autism spectrum disorder: Method › Procedure › Simulation Training
documents.content: Simulation training included instructions, modeling, rehearsal, and feedback applied to the participant's behavior of manipulating the doll in the model. The participant had a doll that represented the participant and the researcher had a doll that represented the parent. The participants were also required to verbalize the steps of the safety skill while manipulating their doll in the model. During simulation training, the model was placed in front of the participant with the toy firearm in a room in the model, and the researcher presented the participant with a scenario. The participant was provided with instructions on what to do with the doll upon the doll finding the gun. The researcher modeled the correct behavior while vocalizing the steps. For example, upon finding the toy gun, the researcher, using her doll, said, "I found a gun! I need to tell dad!" The researcher then took her doll to the dad doll and said, "Dad, there's a gun." The participant then rehearsed the skill with the doll and received feedback from the researcher (praise for correct performance, further instruction for errors). The participant demonstrated the safety skill with the doll three consecutive times with a gun placed in different locations to end the simulation training session. Multiple exemplars were trained by varying the location of the gun, instructions, and parent dolls. One day following training, an in situ assessment was conducted. Up to two booster sessions identical to the initial training session were conducted if the safety skills did not occur during an in situ assessment following the first training session. One day following each booster session, an in situ assessment occurred.

documents.title: Evaluating small-scale simulation training of firearm safety to children with autism spectrum disorder: Method › Procedure › Ist
documents.content: IST occurred if the participant failed to demonstrate the skill 30 s after finding the gun during an in situ assessment following the second simulation training booster session. IST included instructions, modeling, rehearsal, and feedback. When the researcher entered the room, she stopped any activity the participant was engaging in and provided instructions to engage in the target behavior. The researcher modeled the target behavior while vocalizing the steps. The participant then rehearsed the steps, and the researcher provided praise for correct performance and/or corrective feedback consisting of further instruction. When the child ran from the room to tell the parent about the gun, the parent provided enthusiastic praise. The participant demonstrated the safety skill three consecutive times to conclude the IST session. The next day, an in situ assessment occurred, and if the participant did not score 3, further IST sessions occurred, followed 1–3 days later by in situ assessments.

documents.title: Evaluating small-scale simulation training of firearm safety to children with autism spectrum disorder: Method › Procedure › Reinforcement
documents.content: If the participant did not engage in the safety skill after three IST sessions, a reinforcement procedure was used. The researcher conducted a BST session that consisted of multiple role-plays in which the participant (Eric) found a gun, engaged in the safety skills, and received a preferred item as a reinforcer. The preferred item was chosen based on asking the client "What do you want to work for?." During in situ assessments that occurred after the BST session, the participant only had access to the item if he or she engaged in the safety skills. If the participant did not engage in the behavior, he or she received IST but did not receive the item.

documents.title: Evaluating small-scale simulation training of firearm safety to children with autism spectrum disorder: Results
documents.content: Results, as shown in Figure 1, varied for all participants who received small-scale simulation training. Garret touched the firearm during two different in situ assessments and one simulation assessment. During the first in situ assessment, Garret picked up the firearm by the handle and held it in the air. He stayed in the assessment area and did not report the firearm to his parents. During the second in situ assessment, he poked the firearm with his finger and sat next to it. Again, he stayed in the assessment area and did not report the firearm. During both assessments, he made statements to himself about finding a "laser gun." During the simulation assessment, Garret did not touch the firearm, except for dropping his doll on top of it. However, he did pick it up himself. Following simulation training, Garret engaged in the safety responses, scoring 3 for the assessment. After finding the firearm, he stepped back and walked about three feet from the assessment area and yelled to his parents that he found a laser gun. He engaged in similar responses for the following assessments scoring 3. During a simulation assessment, Garret manipulated the doll to engage in the correct response, scoring 3.

documents.title: Evaluating small-scale simulation training of firearm safety to children with autism spectrum disorder: Results
documents.content: Eric had three in situ assessments and two simulation assessments in baseline. During the first in situ assessment, Eric did not touch the firearm; however, he did not leave the area or report it to a parent. He engaged in a similar response during the simulation assessment. He remained in the area without touching the firearm but did not report it. During his second in situ assessment, he picked up the firearm by the handle and held in the air. He then put it down and left the room, scoring 0. During a second simulation assessment, Eric scored 0 by having his doll lay on top of the firearm. During the final baseline in situ assessment, he scored 1. Following simulation training, Eric touched the gun scoring 0. Following a booster session of simulation training, he scored a two by leaving the room. After the final booster session, he scored 1 by remaining seated next to the firearm. IST was conducted immediately after the third in situ assessment in the intervention phase. Following IST, Eric scored 1. Furthermore, IST was conducted and he scored 1 on the next two assessments. When the reinforcement procedure was implemented, he scored 3 on the first and second assessments. On a third assessment, he scored 0 by grazing his finger on the firearm when trying to access a preferred item located beneath the gun. On the fourth assessment he scored 3. He also scored 3 on a simulation assessment.

documents.title: Evaluating small-scale simulation training of firearm safety to children with autism spectrum disorder: Results
documents.content: Mackenzie had five in situ assessments and three simulation assessments during baseline. During the first in situ assessment, Mackenzie scored 1; she remained in the area and did not report finding the firearm, but she did not touch it. Mackenzie picked up the firearm during the second in situ assessment scoring 0. During the third in situ assessment, she remained in the area again scoring 1. During the fourth and fifth in situ assessments, she picked up the firearm scoring 0. During her first simulation assessment, she scored 1. During the second, she picked up the firearm and had her doll pretend to shoot the dad doll, scoring 0. In a third simulation assessment, Mackenzie picked up the firearm scoring 0. Following small-scale simulation training, Mackenzie scored 0 during the first in situ assessment. She picked up the firearm, yelling "There's a gun!" Although she reported the gun, she received 0 due to picking up the firearm. Following a booster session of simulation training, she scored 1. She remained seated with the firearm in front of her. After 30 s had passed, the gun was removed and she quietly said, "It's a gun." A second booster session was conducted. When an in situ assessment was conducted, Mackenzie scored 0 after picking up the firearm. Immediately after the assessment, IST was conducted. During the next in situ assessment Mackenzie scored 0. Additional IST was conducted, and she scored 3 during the next three consecutive in situ assessments. She also scored 3 during a simulation assessment.

documents.title: Evaluating small-scale simulation training of firearm safety to children with autism spectrum disorder: Results
documents.content: Social validity data were collected from three parents using a questionnaire provided at the end of the study. The scores were averaged. Parents strongly agreed that their child enjoyed participating in this study (4.6), believed their child was safer now if he or she finds a gun (4.3), liked using simulation training (4.3), liked using simulation training to teach their child (4.6), would use simulation training to teach their child other skills (4.6), and would recommend simulation training to others (4.6). Side-effect questionnaires were completed by three parents. One parent reported that their child was much more scared of firearms. All parents reported their children were much more cautious and hesitant to touch firearms. Two parents reported that their children were a little more upset and concerned about personal safety. All parents were satisfied with the researcher's communication.

documents.title: Evaluating small-scale simulation training of firearm safety to children with autism spectrum disorder: Discussion
documents.content:
This study investigated the effects of using small-scale simulation training to teach firearm safety skills to children with ASD. Findings from this study suggest that simulation training may be an effective procedure for teaching firearm safety skills for some children. Garret demonstrated the skills during in situ assessments following one session of simulation training. However, it was not an effective procedure for teaching Eric and Mackenzie, and further training was needed to generalize the skill to the natural environment. More research is needed to establish when and for whom small-scale simulation training will be effective and how it may be modified to make it more effective. The results showed that IST was effective for Mackenzie but not for Eric after the failure of small-scale simulation training. For Eric, IST and a reinforcement procedure were needed to promote generalization of the safety skills.

Although none of the parents reported that their children had received any firearm safety training, all of them seemed surprised at the unsafe behaviors the participants engaged in when finding a gun. After Mackenzie's second in situ assessment, her mom reported being shocked that her child would pick up the gun. In addition, during a simulation assessment, Mackenzie had the doll picking up the gun and saying, "I'm going to shoot you, Daddy!" Mackenzie's mom reported to the researcher that she was hesitant to participate at first but "this is the world we live in." After seeing her daughter's behavior, she was happy to continue participation. Furthermore, her responses on the social validity survey suggest that she was happy she participated and thought the training was valuable.

documents.title: Evaluating small-scale simulation training of firearm safety to children with autism spectrum disorder: Discussion
documents.content: The results of this study are different from Maxfield et al. (2019) who showed that small-scale simulation training was effective for typically developing children. In this study, it only worked for one of the three children with ASD. More research is needed to replicate small-scale simulation training with kids with and without ASD to see if it is differentially effective across these groups. The results of this study are similar to results from studies showing that BST is not effective for some children and that IST is effective for some children but not others until an incentive is added (e.g., Hanratty et al., 2016; King & Miltenberger, 2017). King and Miltenberger (2017) showed that, although IST was effective for three participants, one participant needed an added incentive to demonstrate the skill (2017). Hanratty et al. (2016) found that additional contingencies were needed for preschoolers to demonstrate the skill. If a participant did not demonstrate the skill, he or she had to practice for an additional 10 min instead of playing with his or her peers. Furthermore, a time out procedure was needed for one participant. These results show that IST alone is not always effective. An added reinforcement or punishment procedure may be needed. More research is needed to establish the limits of effectiveness of small-scale simulation training and IST for teaching safety skills.

documents.title: Evaluating small-scale simulation training of firearm safety to children with autism spectrum disorder: Discussion
documents.content: It is not clear what variables contributed to the success of small-scale simulation training for Garret. It may be possible that Garret's previous exposure to BST was beneficial in generalizing the behavior of manipulating his doll to engage in safety skills in the model to his own behavior during in situ assessments. In addition, it is unclear why IST was not effective for Eric. Eric had exposure to IST in learning other skills, but often took more sessions to be successful. With more training sessions, IST may have been effective for promoting the generalization of the safety skills for Eric. Researchers have shown that numerous IST sessions are necessary in some cases before the participant exhibits the safety skills consistently during in situ assessments (Johnson et al., 2005). It is also possible that when Eric found the gun, because it was placed next to a preferred item, praise for doing the right thing could not compete with reinforcement from interacting with the preferred item.

documents.title: Evaluating small-scale simulation training of firearm safety to children with autism spectrum disorder: Discussion
documents.content: It is unclear which components of small-scale simulation training were effective in teaching the safety skills to the children in Maxfield et al. (2019) and to Garrett in this study. It is likely that requiring participants to actively engage with their doll and describe the doll's actions and providing feedback based on the doll's performance was necessary for correct responding during in situ assessments. It is also unclear how well-established a child's generalization skills need to be for this type of training to be effective. A repertoire of generalization seems to be an important skill to have for this training to be effective. One focus of future research may be to determine whether children differ with respect to the degree that they have experience learning skills in one context and performing them in another. Although this may be an important skill or learning history to have for this training to be effective, it was not assessed prior to training in this study or any other study to our knowledge.

documents.title: Evaluating small-scale simulation training of firearm safety to children with autism spectrum disorder: Discussion
documents.content: One limitation of this study is the lack of experimental control demonstrated in the multiple baseline across participants design. Because a different procedure was effective for each of the three participants, there was no replication of any one procedure. Nonetheless, even though there is no replication within this study, the effectiveness of each of the three procedures represents replications of published research. Furthermore, we believe that the results are important for showing that small-scale simulation training may not be as effective for children with autism as it appears to be for children without disabilities. However, this finding is tentative; until more research is conducted, we cannot conclude that small-scale simulation is not effective for children with autism. In spite of this limitation, a strength of this study is that it is a model of data-based decision-making in which failure of one approach is detected immediately in the data and leads to the implementation of a more intrusive approach until the skills occur reliably during in situ assessments. Consistent with the literature, this study illustrates that an individualized approach to safety skills training is needed (and in fact is best practice) when working with children with autism.

documents.title: Evaluating small-scale simulation training of firearm safety to children with autism spectrum disorder: Discussion
documents.content:
A second possible limitation is that we evaluated only three small-scale simulation training sessions. It is possible that with more sessions, all children may have exhibited the skills during in situ assessments. However, we chose three training sessions to be consistent with other research evaluating BST for teaching safety skills (e.g., Himle, Miltenberger, Flessner, et al., 2004, Miltenberger et al., 2004). Future research should replicate this study with children with autism with a larger number of small-scale simulation training sessions to see if more training increases effectiveness. If found to be effective, researches should replicate with different target behaviors such as poison and abduction prevention, children of different ages, and with a larger number of children due to the lack of research on small-scale simulation training. Future research could also assess generalization across different environments, such as schools and community. It would also be interesting to evaluate this procedure using dyads, such as siblings, during training and assessments.

In summary, this study demonstrated that small-scale simulation training may be effective for some children with ASD. Although it is unclear why this intervention was effective for one participant and not for others, it has the possibility to teach firearm safety skills in an accessible and inexpensive way.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Introduction
documents.content: According to the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI, 2021) four out of the 10 days with the greatest number of background checks to get firearms have been in 2021 with the top three days being in March alone. Additionally, according to a survey completed by the National Shooting Sports Foundation (NSSF, 2020), 40% of customers at gun shops are first-time customers. According to the FBI, this increase in purchasing firearms in the United States is likely in response to mass shootings along with political unrest such as the insurrection of the U.S. Capitol (FBI, 2021). Unfortunately, with the increase in firearm sales, children are more at risk for accidental shootings. In the United States, one-third of homes have at least one firearm in them (Smith et al., 2015). To keep children safe from accidental shootings, every gun-owning individual should keep their firearms unloaded, locked, and safe from children who could find them; however, gun owners do not always store their guns safely. Of 3000 individuals surveyed at an event in Washington, 40% of those with guns reported that they kept the guns unlocked in their homes even if children were present (King et al., 2017). Unfortunately, research shows that when children find guns, they are likely to play with them (Jackman et al., 2001). In 2021, there were 342 unintentional shootings by children resulting in 219 injuries and 141 deaths of children. In 2020, there were 369 unintentional shootings by children with 142 of those shootings resulting in the death of a child (Everytown, 2021). Fortunately, firearm safety researchers have investigated methods to teach children to respond safely when they find a gun.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Introduction
documents.content: Two training methods that are effective for teaching firearm safety skills to children are behavioral skills training (BST) and in situ training (IST) (Miltenberger, 2008; Miltenberger et al., 2020). During BST the trainer provides the trainee with information on the safety skill, models the safety skill, provides the trainee with the opportunity for multiple rehearsals in role plays, and delivers feedback on the trainee's performance. The feedback includes both descriptive praise for correct performance and corrective feedback (further instruction) for errors. The trainee rehearses the safety skills until they demonstrates all of the safety skills correctly in multiple role plays simulating situations in which the trainee is most likely to encounter the potential danger. In situ training is conducted within the natural environment with the simulated safety threat present (Miltenberger, 2008). With IST an assessment is conducted without the child being aware of the assessment. If the child does not respond correctly, a previously unseen trainer steps in and requires the child to rehearse the safety skill in the in situ assessment environment. In situ training has been the only method of training to produce consistent results for all children during in situ assessments; however, the number of IST sessions required for safety skills generalization is variable. Some trainees require a single session, while others require more (Gatheridge et al., 2004; Himle et al., 2004; Miltenberger et al., 2004). Miltenberger et al. (2004) used IST for children who did not generalize firearm safety skills to the natural environment following BST. The three participants that required IST received anywhere from four to 10 sessions of IST, with one study participant requiring an incentives phase to establish motivation.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Introduction
documents.content: Although BST and IST have been shown to be effective interventions to teach firearm safety skills to children, these training approaches are effortful and time consuming (e.g., Gatheridge et al., 2004; Jostad et al., 2008). Video modeling (VM) and video self-modeling (VSM) are two other training methods that require less time while still promoting generalization of skills (Bellini & Akullian, 2007). Video modeling consists of children watching peers correctly engage in a skill in the proper context. With VSM however, the child acts as the model in the video. Bellini and Akullian (2007) completed a meta-analysis of VM and VSM interventions and found that the median duration of video clips, which is the main component of the intervention, was 3 min across 23 peer-reviewed studies. They also found moderate maintenance and generalization effects for both VM and VSM indicating that these interventions can be effective at promoting generalization. Video modeling has been evaluated for teaching safety skills in a few studies. Godish et al. (2017) evaluated VM for teaching abduction prevention skills to children diagnosed with autism. During intervention, the parents showed their children three videos consisting of a three different children responding safely to three different lures. The results showed that VM was effective; all four participants engaged in the safety skills during in situ assessments. However, other researchers showed VM was not effective for promoting the generalized use of gun safety skills (Morgan & Miltenberger, 2017) and poison safety skills with children with disabilities (King & Miltenberger, 2017).

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Introduction
documents.content:
Although research has evaluated VM to teach safety skills to children, no study has evaluated VSM to teach safety skills even though it has been shown to be effective in teaching other skills (e.g., Cihak & Schrader, 2008; Kurnaz & Yanardag, 2018; Lee et al., 2007; Sadler, 2019). Cihak and Schrader (2008) compared VM to VSM to teach two vocational tasks to four adults with intellectual disabilities. For the skill that was taught using VM, an adult model was used to demonstrate the skills to participants, whereas with VSM the participant themselves acted as the model. Results indicated that both video interventions were effective, however, three participants required fewer sessions to reach criterion when using VSM compared to VM indicating that VSM may be more efficient (Cihak & Schrader, 2008).

Due to the potentially greater efficiency of VM and VSM interventions relative to BST and IST, more research is warranted evaluating video interventions for teaching safety skills. In addition with some studies indicating VM is ineffective (King & Miltenberger, 2017; Morgan & Miltenberger, 2017) and research showing VSM may be more efficient than VM for teaching skills to individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) or intellectual disabilities (Cihak & Schrader, 2008) additional research is warranted to determine if VSM is also effective for teaching safety skills to children with disabilities. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of VSM to teach firearm safety skills to children diagnosed with ASD.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Method › Participants And Setting
documents.content: Five children, ages 5-13 years old, diagnosed with intellectual disabilities were recruited to participate in this study. Rob and Jon were 5-year-old boys, Arya was a 13-year-old girl, Ned was an 8-year-old boy, and Sam was a 6-year-old boy. Potential participants were excluded if they were unable to walk or communicate vocally, due to the need for the participants to leave the area of the firearm independently and inform an adult. Additionally, prior to collecting baseline data, an assessment to determine if participants had the skill set necessary to report a firearm to a caregiver was conducted. Participants were required to report a picture of a common household object (e.g., chair, dresser, bed) from another room to their caregiver. The picture was placed in an empty room of the home, and the participant was told to find the picture, look at it, walk to another room, and tell the researcher what the picture was. Training, assessment, and videotaping for the self-model videos were completed within the participants' homes.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Method › Materials
documents.content: An iPhone X and Apple MacBook was used to develop the self-modeling videos. Tablets or an Apple MacBook were used to show the videos to the participants during training. Each video was approximately 5 min long. Videos had a narrator first describe how to engage in the firearm safety skills, and then a video showed the participant engaging in the skills in three different scenarios. For example, a narrator first described how a child should respond when they find a firearm and then asked the following during an additional clip: "You are about to watch yourself find a gun in your parent's kitchen. What should you do?" Following the clip, a brief pause (approximately 5 s) occurred to allow the participant to respond; after which, the narrator said, "If you said you should say not touch the gun, quickly get away, and tell an adult what just happened, you are correct! Let's Watch!" Researchers used a disabled firearm (i.e., welded barrel, hammer, trigger, and magazine) for in situ assessments.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Method › Target Behaviors And Assessments
documents.content: The target behaviors were not touching the firearm, walking/running away from the firearm to a trusted adult within 10 s of finding the firearm, and reporting the firearm to a trusted adult within 10 s. Target behaviors were scored as follows: 0 = touched the firearm; 1 = did not touch the firearm but failed to leave the area or tell an adult; 2 = did not touch the firearm and got away from it but did not inform an adult 3 = did not touch the firearm, got away from it, and told a trusted adult. In situ assessments were conducted to assess each participant's firearm safety skills pre- and post-training. In situ assessments took place in the participant's home and the participant was not aware that an assessment was taking place. The firearm was placed in a predetermined area of the house that contained a hidden video camera and the parents were instructed to provide the participant a reason to go to the area that the firearm was placed. Precautions were made to ensure that others, not participating in the study, did not interfere during the assessment. If the participant touched the gun or did not leave on their own within 10 s, the caregiver entered the room and instructed the participant to leave the room. If the participant engaged in the safety skills, the caregiver delivered praise to the participant such as "Thank you for telling me! It is important to tell me immediately if you ever find a gun."

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Method › Interobserver Agreement
documents.content: To collect IOA data, two researchers independently watched a streamed video of in situ assessments and scored the participant's performance of the safety skills. We divided the number of agreements on the three target skills by the sum of the agreements and disagreements. An agreement was scored for a target behavior if both researchers scored it as occurring or both recorded it as not occurring. IOA, collected for 35% of assessments across baseline and intervention phases, was 100%.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Method › Social Validity And Side Effects
documents.content: At the conclusion of data collection for each participant, we sent a social validity questionnaire to the caregiver via email and asked the caregiver to complete it and return it via email. This was a 4-item questionnaire that used a 5-point Likert scale ranging from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree." Items included "I believe my child is safer now if he/she finds a gun," "I would recommend this form of training to others," "My child enjoyed participating in this study," and "I liked the procedures used to teach my child." In addition to the social validity questionnaire, we asked caregivers to complete a side-effects questionnaire (also sent via email). The questionnaire was designed to have caregivers inform researchers of any behavioral changes related to firearms after participating in this study. Questions included "Compared to before this study my child now appears scared: afraid to go into rooms that they found guns," "Compared to before this study my child now appears cautious: hesitant to go into rooms alone," and "Compared to before this study my child now appears upset or concerned about the issue of firearms, personal safety, etc." Caregivers were asked to describe any changes related to these questions and were allowed to write in if they observed any other changes that may have been a result of participating.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Method › Experimental Design And Procedure › General
documents.content: This study was reviewed and approved by the University of South Florida's Institutional Review Board. We evaluated VSM in a nonconcurrent multiple baseline design across participants. In situ assessments were used during baseline, after video filming, following training, and at follow-up. Mastery criterion was a score of 3 during three consecutive in situ assessments. If the participant scored lower than a three on an in situ assessment after VSM training, another VSM session (booster training) occurred. If the participant scored lower than a 3 a second time during in situ assessments then IST followed. To assess maintenance of the safety skills, we conducted in situ assessments 2 weeks after VSM training or IST.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Method › Experimental Design And Procedure › Baseline
documents.content: Baseline consisted of in situ assessments. Caregivers were provided with instruction on their role during in situ assessments and no feedback was provided on participant performance during the assessments.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Method › Experimental Design And Procedure › Development Of Self Modeling Videos
documents.content: After baseline data collection, the self-modeling videos were filmed. The videos were created at the participants' homes, so participants saw their behavior in their natural environments. The areas of the house where filming occurred were blocked off to prevent individuals not participating in the study from entering the area. During filming, the researchers recorded one of the three skills at a time in random order, so the participant did not complete the three skills together in sequence. In this way, the participant did not rehearse the safety skills together during filming. During filming, the researchers provided the participants with prompts to complete the behaviors correctly such as "Jon, I want you to walk over to that table and yell 'gun' with your hands up in the air and then walk back to me." Editing software was used to show the participant engaging in the three skills in sequence when finding a gun and to remove evidence of other persons from the video to make it appear the participant completed the skills independently. Additionally, editing software was used to include voiceover narrative of what the participants were doing in the videos. To determine whether prompting participants to execute the skills during the creation of the video led to an increase in performance, we conducted an in situ assessment within a week after filming. If a participant achieved a score of 3, up to two more in situ assessments were conducted. If the participant scored below a 3, the participant moved to the VSM phase. If the participant scored three 3's, the participant moved to the follow-up phase.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Method › Experimental Design And Procedure › Video Self Modeling
documents.content: If participants did not achieve three consecutive scores of 3 during in situ assessments following the filming of the video, they watched the self-modeling video made by the investigator. In the VSM session, the experimenter had the participant sit in a room with no distractions and watch the video on a computer or tablet screen. The videos consisted of an introduction to why guns are dangerous and what the participants should do if they come across a gun. The participants then watched the three scenarios of themselves engaging in the safety skills when finding a gun in three different locations. The experimenter made sure the participant watched the entire video and prompted the participant to respond to the narrator's questions if the participant did not respond independently. All of the participants watched the entire video and responded to the narrator's questions. Each video was approximately 2-3 min in length.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Method › Experimental Design And Procedure › In Situ Training
documents.content: A researcher conducted IST if the participant failed to engage in the safety skills during in situ assessments after a booster VSM training had occurred. The booster VSM session was identical to the first VSM session. During IST, a researcher approached the participant 10 s after the participant failed to engage in the correct responses. The researcher informed the participant what steps they missed, modeled the correct response and had the participant rehearse safety skills in the presence of the firearm. If the participant engaged in all safety steps correctly, the researcher delivered praise. The participants practiced the skills until they performed the steps correctly three consecutive times. An in situ assessment was scheduled 2-3 days after the IST session. Only one IST session was needed for Jon.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Method › Experimental Design And Procedure › Follow Up
documents.content: Two weeks after the participant achieved criterion performance in VSM or IST phases, a follow-up in situ assessment occurred.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Results
documents.content:
Figure 1 shows the results of in situ assessments for baseline, filming the video, VSM, IST, and follow-up. The results show that three participants demonstrated the skills following VSM (Sam, Arya, and Rob), one participant exhibited the skills following VSM and IST (Jon) and one participant (Ned) executed the skills during in situ assessments after participating in filming the video but before watching the video. All participants maintained the target behaviors during the 2-week follow-up assessments.

In baseline all participants touched the gun at least once and Jon and Sam touched the gun in every baseline assessment, demonstrating that these participants were at risk for firearm injury. During the assessment after filming the video there was no increase in the safety skills for Jon, Sam, or Rob. However, the safety skills increased to a score of three in the first assessment after filming for Arya but then fell back to baseline in the second assessment. Finally, for Ned, the safety skills increased to 3 and remained there for all assessments after filming.

When VSM was implemented for Sam, Arya, and Rob, safety skills immediately increased to a score of 3 and remained at 3 for all subsequent assessments. When VSM was implemented for Jon, his safety score increased from 0 to 2 in the first assessment and then to 3 in the second VSM assessment. However, his score decreased to 0 in his third assessment so IST was implemented. Following one IST session, he scored 3 in all subsequent assessments.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Results
documents.content: The social validity questionnaire and the side effects questionnaire were completed by only one participant. The results of the social validity questionnaire indicated that the parents believed their child was safer after completing the study (score of 5 out of 5) and that overall, both the parent (score 5 out of 5) and their child enjoyed participating in the study (score of 4 out of 5). Additionally, the parent reported that they would recommend this training to others, and this parent requested that the video be shown to her two older children to help them teach safety skills. For the side effects questionnaire, the parent reported that there was no observed change in their child's responding related to firearms or going into rooms in which assessments were conducted.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Discussion
documents.content: The results of this study demonstrated that VSM was an effective intervention for three of four participants who viewed the video, VSM followed by IST was effective for one participant, and participating in making the video resulted in successful performance for one individual. Success of the interventions was indicated by performance of the safety skills when finding a gun during three consecutive in situ assessments, thus demonstrating generalization of the skills beyond the training context. These results provide partial support for the effectiveness of VSM as an intervention for promoting the generalized use of gun safety skills. The findings of this research are consistent with existing research on the use of VSM with other skills exhibited by children with autism or other developmental disabilities (Bellini & Akullian, 2007; Kurnaz & Yanardag, 2018; Lee et al., 2007). The results of this study also provide preliminary evidence that VSM may have an equal or greater degree of effectiveness than BST which has been shown to be effective for teaching gun safety skills in about half of the participants across studies (e.g., Himle et al., 2004; Miltenberger et al., 2004; Novotny et al., 2020). Consistent with research on BST and IST for promoting the generalized use of gun safety skills, IST was effective in this study when VSM was not effective. Although the results of this research are promising, more research is needed evaluating VSM to establish its effectiveness for promoting the generalized use of gun-safety skills and other safety skills among individuals with disabilities.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Discussion
documents.content:
A further finding from this study was that one participant engaged in the safety skills during in situ assessments after being filmed engaging in the safety skills while the researchers made the self-modeling video.

Interestingly, participating in filming the video resulted in the use of the safety skills even though the participant engaged in each of the three skills independently and in random order and never executed the skills together in proper order while the researcher made the video.

A strength of this study was evaluating safety skills after making the video but before viewing it as a way to evaluate the relative effects of engaging in the component skills during filming versus viewing themselves engaging in the safety skills in response to finding a gun in the self-modeling video.

It is not clear why the participant engaged in the safety skills during in situ assessments after participating in filming the video.

The most likely explanation is that engaging in each of the three behaviors was akin to the rehearsal component of BST.

Although we attempted to minimize the likelihood that making the video would be an active intervention process by separating the three safety steps and never practicing them in sequence or in the order they are used, nonetheless, executing the skills during training did constitute practice.

Our recommendation for future research in VSM is to have the participant engage in the safety steps in random order while filming, executing one step per day separated by multiple days, and evaluating the effects of making the video for the VSM intervention multiple days after filming.

In this way, the process of filming the participant is less likely to influence the execution of the skills and researchers can more cleanly evaluate the effects of VSM.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Discussion
documents.content:
However, we have different recommendation for clinical practice in the use of VSM.

In clinical practice, the goal would be beneficial behavior change for the participant in which the process of making the video would be seen as a component of the intervention an opportunity to influence the safety skills and not a process to control as a possible confounding variable.

Therefore, in making the video, the participant should rehearse the skills in proper sequence with praise and corrective feedback so making the video is equivalent to a BST session.

Because the goal of clinical practice would not be to parse the effects of BST and VSM to demonstrate experimental control, combining these procedures would not be an issue and would constitute best practice.

This practice would essentially constitute BST plus VSM and the value would be to get the initial effects of BST, the added effects of watching the video, and the possible enduring effects that might come from watching the video at periodic intervals after training to help promote maintenance.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Discussion
documents.content:
One limitation of the current study is that only one caregiver completed the social validity and side effects questionnaire.

Future research should further evaluate parents' acceptability of VSM and determine if any side effects are observed from the training.

We have a number of recommendations for future research on VSM as an intervention for teaching safety skills.

First, research should replicate this study and evaluate VSM with individuals with ID with similar ages and ability levels as the participants in this study to evaluate the robustness of our findings.

Second, researchers should replicate this study with individuals with ID of varying ages and ability levels and with neurotypical children.

Third, researchers should evaluate VSM with other safety skills with individuals with ID and neurotypical children.

In particular, evaluating VSM with other physical safety threats (e.g., poisons or fire starting agents) and social safety threats (e.g., sexual abuse or abduction) in which the participant must respond safely to lures from adults is important to establish the generality of the intervention.

Fourth, researchers should take steps to minimize the effects of making the video (as described earlier) when evaluating VSM and should always assess safety skills after making the video but before the participant views it, to evaluate the effects of making the video.

Fifth, researchers should conduct research to compare the effects of VSM and BST.

This study suggests VSM might be more effective than BST as research shows that BST is effective about half the time (Baruni & Miltenberger, in press), but the results are preliminary because we did not directly compare the two procedures, and more research is needed.

In addition to comparing the effectiveness of VSM versus BST, future research should also compare the efficiency of the two approaches.

documents.title: Evaluation of video self-modeling to teach firearm safety skills: Discussion
documents.content:
Finally, researchers should evaluate the combination of BST and VSM in which BST is used during filming to make the video used in VSM.

This combined use of BST and VSM would be just as efficient as VSM alone because it would not take any more time to film the participant while conducting BST than is currently needed to film the safety skills steps when making the VSM video.

In the current study, it took about 1-2 h to film the participants and 1 h to edit the video clips into the VSM video.

If the participant participated in BST and engaged in the safety skills in sequence in each rehearsal trial as part of the video filming process, the time required to make the video might be even less.

In summary, this study showed that VSM was an effective intervention for three of four participants, indicating that it may be equally or more effective than BST for teaching safety skills. Although this is a preliminary finding from four participants and more research is need to establish the robustness of VSM, we are encouraged that VSM or BST combined with VSM hold promise as effective interventions for safety skills.

documents.title: Firearms, Physicians, Families, and Kids- Finding Words that Work: Introduction
documents.content:
In 2020, firearm injuries were the leading cause of death in Americans 18 years old and younger, accounting for 3230 children's deaths (63.2% homicide; 30.0% suicide; 4.2% unintentional injury, 2.2% undetermined, and 0.4% legal intervention). This has increased over the last 2 years, concurrent with a surge in firearm purchases and the onset of the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic. Firearms are the most lethal method of suicide attempt, with a case fatality rate of 90%; they account for 42% of suicide deaths among those <19 years of age. Triple-safe storage practices (storing firearms locked and unloaded with ammunition stored separately) are protective, with simulation models demonstrating that even a modest increase in safe storage could lead to decreased rates of suicide and unintentional injury among children and adolescents. The role of safe storage in preventing assaultive injuries has not been established, although we would also expect these to decrease if youth have decreased access to firearms in the home.

Health care providers (HCPs) are well positioned to discuss evidence-based strategies to reduce unauthorized children's access to firearms and minimize the risk of firearm injury. HCPs caring for children are particularly poised to have these conversations, given their role in safety conversations with parents on other topics. Caregivers generally accept firearm safety discussions in pediatric settings; however, many pediatricians do not counsel about firearm injury prevention. Although they believe that counseling may reduce firearm-related injury and death, they cite their lack of knowledge, self-efficacy, and ability to have productive conversations as limitations. The political climate around firearms, lack of HCP training, and absence of a shared language between firearm owners and nonfirearm owners are other barriers that HCPs face.

documents.title: Firearms, Physicians, Families, and Kids- Finding Words that Work: Introduction
documents.content: The challenge to discussing safe firearm storage lies in finding a common language and navigating a productive discussion. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that HCPs discuss with parents of children and adolescents the need to secure firearms to avoid unauthorized access, based on evidence that brief counseling may improve storage practices in homes with children. Specific recommendations include asking about access inside the home and off property and exploring strategies to minimize access. An online educational module based on these principles is available and contains simulations with sample language and strategies to address potential obstacles to such a conversation. Expert suggestions for "culturally respectful, conversation-promoting language" regarding firearm discussions in the general population were described. Here, we build on this knowledge and propose a framework for firearm safety discussions in families with children. We review current evidence and expert opinion, and we suggest best practices for pediatricians to engage families in a patient-centered manner when discussing firearm safety. We suggest specific terminology that can be used during these conversations (Table), recognizing that these have not yet been tested in the real-world setting, and that future refinement is needed as research in the field advances.

documents.title: Firearms, Physicians, Families, and Kids- Finding Words that Work: Setting The Stage For A Nonjudgmental Conversation
documents.content:
Patient-centered care, which is more effective at increasing parental satisfaction and follow-through with treatment plans, generally entails reserving judgment, listening to the patient, building partnership, sharing information, and showing empathy. HCPs are trained in how to talk with their patients about sensitive topics like sexual activity, substance use, and end-of-life care; similarly, HCPs can learn to discuss firearm safety based on these principles.

Nonjudgmental communication is a necessary precursor to any effective conversation about safe firearm storage. To be credible safety messengers, providers need to recognize their own verbal and nonverbal expressions of judgment and implicit biases and avoid introducing them into the conversation and alienating the patient. Families endorse feeling judged or "criminalized" if they feel their physician is making assumptions about their firearm ownership, which can lead to decreased acceptance of safety messaging.

documents.title: Firearms, Physicians, Families, and Kids- Finding Words that Work: Setting The Stage For A Nonjudgmental Conversation
documents.content:
Listening to the caregiver's perspective allows the HCP to counsel the family about safe firearm storage and provide guidance based on their values and beliefs. For injury prevention and anticipatory guidance, this may mean employing a harm reduction approach by tailoring interventions to the individual (eg, use of locking devices) rather than encouraging complete elimination of risk (eg, removing firearms from home permanently). One example of this in adolescent health care is guidance about adolescent sexual activity and counsel around prevention of sexually transmitted infections and unwanted pregnancy, rather than encouraging (or assuming) abstinence. A similar approach may be more acceptable in firearm safety discussions. Families may own a gun for protection and therefore want rapid access. In that setting, the gold standard "Triple-Safe" storage (firearms locked, unloaded, and with ammunition locked separately) endorsed by the American Academy of Pediatrics and National Shooting Sport Foundation is not practical for their circumstances. Nonjudgmental communication and considering a patient's values requires working together to identify an acceptable strategy, such as storing a loaded firearm in a quick-access safe (instead of in an unlocked bedside table).

The strategy of eliciting patient's beliefs and values before counseling is also a central component of motivational interviewing. This approach requires identifying the patient's barriers to change and the associated costs and benefits of their choice, with motivation to change then coming from the patient rather than being imposed by the provider. Motivational interviewing has been effective in changing risk behaviors in the health care setting in general and firearm storage in the pediatric primary care setting specifically, and is well-aligned with patient-centered care recommendations.

documents.title: Firearms, Physicians, Families, and Kids- Finding Words that Work: Setting The Stage For A Nonjudgmental Conversation
documents.content: Another important element of patient-centered care is developing a partnership with families. Placing the conversation in context of safety rather than being about the firearm creates a partnership centered on the common goal of protecting their child. Assessing the caregiver's response and working together to identify the most acceptable means of limiting access is most likely to achieve maximal harm reduction. Finally, given that caregivers tend to underestimate their child's access, HCP should develop partnerships with the youth as well, asking adolescents directly about their access to on and off-property firearms.

documents.title: Firearms, Physicians, Families, and Kids- Finding Words that Work: Universal Delivery Of Firearm Safety Messaging
documents.content:
Rather than asking screening questions ("do you have a firearm in the home?") before counseling, HCPs could consider universal firearm safety messaging—ie, delivering the same message to all families, whether or not there are firearms in the home—a strategy that is viewed favorably by both caregivers and providers.

One of the benefits to this approach is that it addresses some patient concerns of privacy infringement, particularly in communities that place greater value on privacy issues in general.

Individuals have expressed concern about firearm ownership being documented in the medical record, with concerns that it might lead to a federal registry of firearms.

We also know that patients may not disclose information to their providers if they are embarrassed or feel they might be judged or lectured on their behavior.

Because this is a concern among firearm owners, providers risk missing families who do not disclose firearm ownership if they do not discuss safe firearm storage with everyone.

Providing the same message to everyone can be inclusive of nonfirearm owners by providing advice on asking others about safe storage in any place where their children may encounter a firearm, such as at a friend or family's house.

By providing all patients with similar information, providers will capture more firearm owners in their safety conversations.

In addition, they will be able to more broadly distribute educational materials, safe storage messaging, and locking devices to communities.

This approach is also more acceptable to firearm owners.

This does not mean that providers should not address specific risk factors after explaining that firearms are discussed "across the board," describing the specific risks knowing the child's age and circumstance is appropriate.

documents.title: Firearms, Physicians, Families, and Kids- Finding Words that Work: Universal Delivery Of Firearm Safety Messaging
documents.content: For example, The HCP can discuss the risk of accidental injury for an 8-year-old child, or temporary removal of firearms from the home if an adolescent is contemplating suicide.

documents.title: Firearms, Physicians, Families, and Kids- Finding Words that Work: Tailoring The Discussion To Patients Age And Risk Factors
documents.content:
The HCP should place firearm safety counseling into the context of general anticipatory guidance relevant to the child's age and circumstance. If the patient is a toddler, the HCP can discuss car seats and bicycle helmet use; for an adolescent, the provider can review seatbelts and driving. Then, after initiating the conversation with a normative statement (eg, "many families keep a firearm in or near their home"), the HCP should move along to an age-appropriate discussion of firearm safety.

Unintentional firearm injuries are more common among younger children (aged 1–9 years) than older children and adolescents. Among children who die from an unintentional firearm injury, the most common circumstances are playing with the gun, unintentionally pulling the trigger, not knowing that the gun was loaded, and showing the gun to others. Caregivers may assume that their child can or will not access a home firearm, but previous studies have shown that parents underestimate their child's knowledge about whether they have a firearm, whether they have handled it, and its location in the home. These concerns can be relayed to caregivers after initiating a conversation and prior to development of a patient-centered firearm storage plan.

In contrast, in adolescence (10–19 years old), nearly 97% of fatal firearm injuries are intentional homicide or suicide. Discussions of safe firearm storage with youth and their caregivers in this demographic should be presented as a preventive approach for self-harm and assault. The approach to engaging patients and their families, however, varies depending on the reason for firearm ownership and the child's age and risk factors.

documents.title: Firearms, Physicians, Families, and Kids- Finding Words that Work: Tailoring The Discussion To Patients Age And Risk Factors
documents.content:
Discussing the increased risk of suicide death with a home firearm that is not stored safely (locked, unloaded, and with ammunition stored separately) is particularly important in youth with existing mental health disorders, as they are at greater risk for self-harm than their peers. Despite this increased risk, and the evidence supporting lethal means safety as an effective suicide prevention strategy, homes with greater risk youth are not more likely to store firearms in safer ways compared with homes without greater-risk youth. This is likely due to caregivers underestimating their child's risk of suicide or access to home firearms. For suicide prevention, "means safety" is preferred to "means restriction," with improved intended uptake with the former. If there is particularly high-risk situation of an adolescent with suicidal thoughts or ideation, the physician should discuss removal of firearms from the home, emphasizing that it is voluntary and temporary. Addressing access to other potential means such as medications or home hazards helps allay the concern that the physician is singling out firearms.

Adolescents, whose decision-making capacity is more advanced than that of younger children, should be engaged directly in the discussion about firearm access, whether or not there is a gun in the home. This is important because they are frequently able to access firearms with or without their parents' knowledge, and need to understand the dangers of, and alternatives to, doing so. Conversations between HCPs and adolescents are effective at changing attitudes and participation in other risky behaviors, and they would likely promote safer behaviors with respect to firearms.

documents.title: Firearms, Physicians, Families, and Kids- Finding Words that Work: Tailoring The Discussion To Patients Age And Risk Factors
documents.content: Discussing firearms with adolescents is nuanced, albeit sometimes for different reasons. Their grasp of abstract concepts and ability to envision long-term impact of their actions is not fully developed and, like adults, they may be less willing to disclose behaviors they perceive to be embarrassing. The first step in gaining their trust is to interview the adolescent alone, ensure confidentiality (provided there is no imminent risk to the patient or others), and avoid judgment. As with caregivers, it is helpful to normalize the conversation when addressing firearm access. This can be achieved with an opening statement such as, "a lot of kids your age can access a gun... do you have a gun or think you can get one?" For adolescents who have easy access to firearms, the clinician may be able to provide counseling about the dangers of firearms. If the provider is concerned that there is imminent harm to the patient or others, it is appropriate to garner additional support (eg, mental health, social work, violence prevention experts) as indicated.

documents.title: Firearms, Physicians, Families, and Kids- Finding Words that Work: Tailoring The Discussion To Patients Age And Risk Factors
documents.content: Whereas one-third of firearm deaths in youth from 1999 to 2016 were self-inflicted, assault was the most common intent of fatal firearm injuries, accounting for 87% of youth homicides. This potential for violence against others should be addressed with caregivers of older children in addition to the concern for self-harm. Engaging parents and youth in discussing firearm violence should assess both adolescent firearm carriage, as well as risk factors for carriage such as violence exposure. Theoretically, decreasing access should reduce interpersonal firearm violence, but further research is needed to determine whether this is true and which interventions are effective at decreasing intentional injuries by firearm (ie, HCP counseling, hospital-based violence interruption programs, or community-based violence interruption programs). Although variations exist in type and intent of injury based on sex, race, rural-urban living, and other demographic characteristics, we would caution against limiting firearm safety discussions based on these population-level data. Doing so risks missing opportunities to counsel youth and their families based on their individual risk factors.

documents.title: Firearms, Physicians, Families, and Kids- Finding Words that Work: Summary Recommendations
documents.content: Based on the evidence to date, we recommend the following to HCPs when discussing firearms with patients: Leaving aside their personal beliefs and be aware of their own biases around firearms, providing nonjudgmental communication and harm reduction strategies using principles of patient-centered care, considering providing all caregivers with safe firearm storage information that is not contingent on screening, and tailoring additional discussions toward suicide, homicide, or unintentional injury depending on patient age (toddler vs adolescent) and circumstance.

documents.title: Firearms, Physicians, Families, and Kids- Finding Words that Work: Table Content
documents.content:
Instead Of: Starting a conversation with 'do you have firearms?' or Focusing your safety conversation solely on firearms.
Try To: Start with a normative statement such as 'I ask everyone about firearms' or 'many of my patients have firearms.' Address other age-appropriate injury prevention issues in the same conversation.
Rationale: Parents may feel judged if asked about firearm ownership. This can be allayed by explaining that you have these conversations with all patients. Including other injury prevention topics is more acceptable and effective, framing the conversation as a safety issue rather than a firearm issue.

---

Instead Of: Asking 'are your firearms locked up with ammunition stored separately?' or Asking whether there are firearms in the home and only providing education to those who say 'yes.'
Try To: Ask what the owner is doing to prevent access by children or adolescents. Speak to all families about safe firearm storage and asking about guns where their children spend time.
Rationale: This reinforces that the conversation is about child safety. It also provides a starting point for a conversation about decreasing access using shared decision-making, if keeping firearms locked separately from ammunition is not feasible for their intended purpose. Caregivers may be worried about their privacy and not disclose that they have firearms in the home. This ensures that the necessary information still reaches them.

---

Instead Of: Asking 'Would you like a storage lock?' or Using terminology you are unfamiliar with or attempting to answer questions that are beyond your scope.
Try To: Ask 'How many locking devices would you like?' Provide educational materials and discuss safe storage practices.
Rationale: This normalizes firearm ownership and may make the parent more receptive to safety education and to take a device. The HCP is not expected to be a firearm expert, but is a child safety expert.

---

Instead Of: Discussing only firearms when addressing limiting access to lethal means for suicide. Excluding youth from firearm safety discussions. Just providing safe firearm storage information to a youth who reports carrying a firearm.
Try To: Discuss strategies for limiting access to firearms, medications, and other potentially lethal means. Ask both parents and youth about their access to firearms. Ask about reasons the adolescent feels unsafe and determine whether it is within their own home or in the community. Engage child services, a trusted adult, or community resources depending on the situation.
Rationale: Providing this context reinforces that you are counseling best on best practices for suicide prevention and not 'picking on guns.' Parents may underestimate their child's access to firearms, and access is more relevant than the specific storage strategy. Carrying a firearm for protection is a sign that the youth may be involved with drug activities, street gangs, feel threatened by others, or may feel unsafe in their own home.

documents.title: Talking About Firearm Injury and Gun Violence- Words Matter: Introduction
documents.content: For decades, discussions of the prevention of firearm injury have been stalled by the debate between gun rights and gun control. Over time, terminology has developed unintended connotations. "Gun violence" is often viewed as code for "gun control" by gun owners, who may feel blamed or disrespected. Conversely, "firearm injury" is preferred in academic and public health circles as a neutral term encompassing all injury types, though it may be less understood by the general public. Differences in terminology impact public health interventions, patient care, and research. With new funding available for firearm injury prevention, professionals need a shared language to overcome institutional barriers and build trust. Just as health professionals learn to discuss sensitive topics like substance use or sexual orientation, they must learn culturally respectful language regarding firearms.

documents.title: Talking About Firearm Injury and Gun Violence- Words Matter: Language Around Firearms Ownership And Storage
documents.content: Approximately 44% of US adults live in a home with a firearm, with ownership often tied to identity and personal freedom. The most common reason for ownership is personal protection (63%), followed by hunting (40%). "Gun culture" varies geographically and politically, and professionals should avoiding making assumptions based on demographics. The authors suggest using "firearm" rather than "weapon" and acknowledging the strong sense of personal responsibility among owners. Regarding storage, "locked" can be interpreted differently. Devices range from cable locks (unloaded) to quick-access safes (loaded). For owners prioritizing defense, "staging" firearms in quick-access safes may be more acceptable than traditional "locking" methods. Injury prevention discussions should encourage autonomous decision-making.

documents.title: Talking About Firearm Injury and Gun Violence- Words Matter: Language Around Suicide And Firearms
documents.content: Firearms are the most common method of suicide in the US (50% of fatalities), and suicide accounts for 60% of all firearm deaths. The link is due to the high lethality of firearms (90% fatality rate) and the short duration of suicidal crises. Prevention involves reducing access to lethal means, termed "means safety." Counseling should emphasize voluntary and temporary reductions in access, such as off-site storage or locking devices. Language should avoid stigma: use "died by suicide" instead of "committed suicide" (which implies criminality). Avoid terms like "successful" or "failed" suicide attempt. Messaging should emphasize hope and the fact that most attempt survivors do not later die by suicide.

documents.title: Talking About Firearm Injury and Gun Violence- Words Matter: Language Around Community Violence And Firearms
documents.content: Community violence is the intentional use of force between unrelated individuals. Homicide disproportionately affects young Black and Latino men due to structural racism and inequities. Exposure to violence increases the risk of both victimization and perpetration. Trauma-informed care is essential, avoiding criminalizing terms like "gang bangers" or blaming victims. At the community level, messaging should recognize complex structural risk factors rather than attributing violence solely to individual choices or demographics.

documents.title: Talking About Firearm Injury and Gun Violence- Words Matter: Conversation Collaboration And Path Forward
documents.content: Conversations about firearm injury are sensitive due to political, cultural, and disciplinary differences. A growing movement exists for collaboration across the political spectrum. Successful change requires a common, shared language and engagement with those who have "lived experiences." Examples of collaboration include the NSSF-AFSP partnership on suicide prevention and the Health Alliance for Violence Intervention. Tailored messaging is also needed for specific contexts like mass shootings (avoiding naming perpetrators) and intimate partner violence. Mutual understanding of language can help professionals and the public work together to prevent injuries.

documents.title: Talking About Firearm Injury and Gun Violence- Words Matter: Box 1 Recommended Terminology
documents.content:
Category: Firearms and firearm ownership
Rather Than: "Gun"
Consider: "Firearm"
Rationale: "Firearm" may be more neutral

---

Category: Firearms and firearm ownership
Rather Than: "Restriction," "surrender," or "confiscation"
Consider: "Transfer," "relinquishment," or "temporary removal"
Rationale: Avoids provocative language; distinguishes between enforcement and voluntary actions

---

Category: Firearms and firearm ownership
Rather Than: "Assault weapon," "assault rifle," or "military-style rifle"
Consider: "AR15-style rifle," "AK-style rifle," "semiautomatic rifle," "Rifle"
Rationale: Avoids terms that gun owners may perceive as pejorative or inaccurate

---

Category: Firearms and firearm ownership
Rather Than: "Firearm safety counseling"
Consider: "Firearm responsibility," "prevention of unauthorized access," or "secure firearm storage" counseling
Rationale: "Firearm safety" connotes safe handling (usage); focusing on access avoids linkage to storage-related laws

---

Category: Firearms and firearm ownership
Rather Than: "Are your firearms locked up?"
Consider: "Do you prevent access of your firearms by unauthorized individuals" (e.g., untrained, children, at-risk persons)
Rationale: Shifts focus from the item to the at-risk user, drawing on responsible ownership principles

---

Category: Firearms and firearm ownership
Rather Than: "All guns should be stored unloaded and separate from ammunition"
Consider: Responsibly "stage" firearms intended for defensive purposes; responsibly "store" firearms used for hunting or recreation
Rationale: Acknowledges that norms vary by use (e.g., personal defense weapons are often stored locked but loaded)

---

Category: Suicide
Rather Than: "Commit" suicide
Consider: "Die by" or "die of" suicide
Rationale: "Commit" implies criminality and assigns blame

---

Category: Suicide
Rather Than: "Successful" or "failed" suicide attempt
Consider: "Died by suicide," "completed suicide," "killed themselves," "survived an attempt"
Rationale: Avoids assigning moral judgment or implying death is a "good" outcome

---

Category: Suicide
Rather Than: "X caused the suicide"; "it was out of the blue"
Consider: Acknowledge that suicide is complex with no single cause and that there are often warning signs
Rationale: Avoids oversimplifying suicide and encourages awareness

---

Category: Suicide
Rather Than: "Suicide is inevitable"; "they'll always find a way"
Consider: Acknowledge that suicide can be prevented; emphasize hope and providing help
Rationale: Supports rationale for reducing access to lethal means during risk periods

---

Category: Community violence
Rather Than: "Gangs," "thugs," "gang bangers," or "ex-convicts"
Consider: "Group involved," "street affiliated," "formerly incarcerated," "justice involved," or "people who use violence"
Rationale: Avoids stigmatizing based on prior criminality; avoids implying victims "deserved it"

---

Category: Community violence
Rather Than: "Black-on-Black crime"
Consider: Describe the high relative risk of firearm injury among young Black men and the structural racism underlying it
Rationale: Avoids implying inherent racial differences are the risk factor rather than structural inequities

---

Category: Community violence
Rather Than: "Inner cities" or "urban communities" (as code for race)
Consider: Talk about "communities that are disproportionately affected by violence"
Rationale: Avoids stigmatizing people living in urban communities

---

Category: Community violence
Rather Than: Jokes; suggesting victims are withholding information
Consider: Say "I'm sorry this happened to you" and provide space to discuss when ready
